transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, Doctor, nice to meet you. I suppose... I suppose I'm here because I'm just flat-out exhausted. And I don't mean the kind of tired you get from a hard day's work, you know? I worked hard my whole life, I know what physical tired is. This is... this is different. 

It's my workshop, for one. I've got this beautiful setup out back, built the shed myself years ago. Got my table saw, all my hand tools, everything exactly where I want it. I used to spend hours out there, just tinkering, making little things for the grandkids or fixing up old chairs. But for a good while now, I just keep steering completely clear of it. I'll walk out to the yard, look at the door, and I just turn right back around. I can't even bring myself to go inside. 

And then... then there's the family gatherings. My wife, she loves getting everyone together, or going over to my sister's place for a Sunday dinner or a cookout. But I find myself doing this whole routine where I have to figure out if my brother-in-law is going to be there. I'll make my wife call and casually check the guest list, and if there's even a chance he might show up, I won't go. I'll make up an excuse about my knees acting up or say I'm catching a cold. 

I'm 76 years old, Doc. I should be enjoying my time, but instead, I'm doing all these mental gymnastics. After all this time, I'm just so tired of planning my entire life around not running into those reminders. I'm mapping out my days just to avoid my own backyard and my own family get-togethers, and I just... I can't keep living like that.
Doctor: You mentioned avoiding your workshop and family gatherings. Have you lost interest in activities that you used to enjoy, like tinkering in your workshop or spending time with family?

No, no, that’s the thing of it, Doc. That’s what makes it so darn frustrating, if I’m being honest. I haven't lost interest at all. Not one bit. Take the workshop, for instance. I sit there at the kitchen table in the mornings with my coffee—black, just the way I've drank it for fifty years—and I look out the window at that shed, and my hands practically itch to get back to work. Just last week, my eldest daughter, she brought over this beautiful old oak rocking chair. Said she found it at an antique fair, but it’s got a loose spindle on the left side and the seat needs a good sanding and refinishing. I know exactly how to fix it, too. I've got the clamps, the wood glue, the right grit sandpaper just sitting on my workbench waiting for me. I can picture the whole process in my head, and I really, truly want to get out there and make it look brand new for her. I love that kind of work. I always have. 

And it’s the exact same story with the family get-togethers. I miss them terribly! My sister, she hosts these Sunday dinners, and let me tell you, she makes a pot roast that would bring a tear to your eye. Slow cooks it all day with the little red potatoes and the thick cut carrots, exactly the way our mother used to make it back in the day. I love sitting in her living room, listening to the grandkids run around making a racket, sneaking the dog a piece of meat when my sister isn't looking. I want to be there for all of that. I really do. 

So it’s definitely not that I don’t care anymore or that I’ve lost my passion for my hobbies or my folks. It’s just... it’s like I said, it’s that invisible wall I hit. I want to fix that chair, but I can't make myself open the shed door. I want to eat that pot roast and see the kids, but if I know he's gonna be sitting across the table... I just can't do it. So, no, the interest is still there, loud and clear, it's just... well, I'm just stuck.
Doctor: When you think about going into your workshop or attending a family gathering, do you find yourself having upsetting thoughts or memories that come to mind unexpectedly?

Well, Doc, it's not even just when I think about the workshop or the family dinners. That's the part that really gets to me. It's... it's like my own mind is playing tricks on me, and I don't even have to be trying to go out to the shed for it to happen. I could just be going about my day, you know? Just regular, everyday things. Like, I'll be standing at the bathroom sink in the morning, right? Got the hot water running, shaving cream on my face—I still use the old brush and mug, none of that aerosol stuff for me—and I'm just looking in the mirror, trying to get a close shave around the chin, and then, bam. Out of absolutely nowhere, it just hits me. 

I'll see it clear as day. I'll see his hand... his hand holding that heavy tool. It's like a photograph just flashes right behind my eyes, or like someone suddenly turned on a movie projector in my head for a split second. And it's not just a fuzzy memory, Doc, it's sharp. I can see the grip, the way his knuckles looked, the weight of the thing. And it doesn't just happen when I'm shaving, either. I've taken up a bit of watercolor painting recently—just small landscapes, you know, trying to keep my hands busy indoors since I can't go to the workshop—and I'll be sitting there, perfectly calm, mixing up a nice shade of green for a pine tree, and suddenly, there it is again. That same image. His hand. That tool. 

And I'll tell you, when it pops into my head like that, completely uninvited, it's not just a thought I can brush away. My whole body reacts to it. My chest... it just seizes up. It gets so tight, like someone wrapped a thick leather belt around my ribs and pulled it as hard as they could. I have to put down my razor, or my paintbrush, and just grip the edge of the sink or the table and take these deep, ragged breaths until the tightness passes. It's exhausting, having these pictures just jump out at you when you're least expecting it, when you're just trying to live a quiet life. So, yes, the thoughts are there, but they don't even wait for me to think about the workshop or my brother-in-law. They just... they just barge right in whenever they please.
